belief: My best years are behind me.
origins: Nostalgia is natural, but it can harden into believing that the good is over. Losses of health, spouse, or work make the past glow and the future dim.
teaches: Solomon cautions that it is unwise to ask why the old days were better than these (Ecclesiastes 7:10), and says God “has made everything beautiful in its time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Paul, near the end of life, wrote, “Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal.” Jeremiah’s lament says of the LORD’s mercies, “They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!” Gratitude for the past and anticipation for what God still has can live together.
self_statements: The future has nothing for me.
I just wait for the end.
errors: Believing the past was all good and the present is all bad.
Predicting that nothing good lies ahead.
Feeling nostalgic and concluding the best is gone.
questions: What made those years so good, and can any of it be found now?
What good things am I experiencing today?
What new thing could I try?
What does God say about new mercies?
What do I look forward to?
Whom might I bless with my experience?
truth: I can thank God for the past and still look for His goodness today. God makes things beautiful in their time, and His mercies are new each morning.
hw_truths: God made everything beautiful in its time.
His mercies are new every morning.
I press on toward what is ahead.
log: Each day, name one good thing about today.
actions: Write the blessings of the past with thanks.
Take a class, visit a place, or meet someone.
Share them with a grandchild or friend.
prayer: Lord, I treasure the past, but let me not miss today. Open my eyes to the good You are doing now and give me hope for what lies ahead. Amen.
